children.translated_text: For the liberation of all beings,
the vision of the path to <s>mukti</s> (liberation),
O Lord of Gods, the knowledge and conduct —
please tell me out of compassion.
O beautiful one, <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) and <s>ācāra</s> (conduct)
I shall now teach you,
by which the knowers enter <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation),
their impurities destroyed.
Those in whom has arisen, through awakening,
knowledge of time, O fair-faced one —
for them no awakening arises
even from hundreds of crores of <s>śāstras</s> (scriptures).
Therefore, the wise one should be fearless,
free from doubt, devoid of craving,
devoted to the enthusiasm of <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge),
faithful and untroubled.
Free from possessiveness, endowed with compassion,
granting fearlessness to all beings —
one should practice the <s>Kālottara</s>, O <s>Devī</s>,
the seeker of liberation, devoted to <s>yoga</s>.
He is <s>Brahmā</s>, he is <s>Śiva</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>,
he is <s>Indra</s>, he is <s>Ṣaḍānana</s> (the six-faced one),
he is the <s>Guru</s> and all the gods,
he is the <s>yogī</s>, he is rich in <s>tapas</s> (austerity),
he is the learned one, the greatly fortunate,
truly fulfilled in the highest sense —
he by whom the mind, restless like the moving wind,
is held steady and motionless.
That is the means to liberation,
that one possesses truly acquired virtues;
that is wisdom, that is steadfastness here,
that is the merit of the resolute.
That alone is pilgrimage, that is charity,
that is <s>tapas</s> (austerity) — there is no doubt.
The means by which the mind, made restless
by the winds, is bound from wavering —
when the mind is restless, there is <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly bondage);
when motionless, that is <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) indeed.
Therefore, the wise one should make the mind steady
through the highest <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom).
Where there is singular bliss
and likewise absolute bliss,
in the supreme <s>tattva</s> (reality) beyond all action —
what wise person would not be attracted?
Turned away from sense-knowledge,
devoted to partless knowledge,
the intelligent one, even without desiring,
attains imperishable <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation).
Consciousness conjoined with the trace of 'I-ness'
is called <s>sakala</s> (with parts).
Consciousness devoid of 'I-ness'
is called <s>caitanya</s> as <s>Śakti</s> (power).
The universe thus illuminated
is declared to be meditation on <s>Śakti</s>.
That which is free from all supports
is called <s>niṣkala</s> (partless) knowledge.
That which is void of the 'I' aspect,
pure awareness-light alone, non-dual —
that is declared the seed of liberation,
the initiator of the supreme <s>yoga</s>.
<s>Cakras</s> (energy centers), <s>nāḍīs</s> (channels), lotuses,
deities, seed-syllables, <s>maṇḍalas</s> (sacred diagrams),
forms and such things —
none of these should ever be meditated upon.
Trickery, nets of <s>mantras</s>,
<s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control) and <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration) —
none of this should be practiced
by one who desires imperishable liberation.
Here there is no worship, no obeisance,
no <s>japa</s> (recitation), nor meditation either.
Only <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge) is proclaimed;
there is nothing else to be known.
For those whose minds are directed outward,
causes of bondage arise.
By restraining the outward-directed mind,
the wise one does not suffer in the world.
Here there is nothing external, nothing internal,
no middle, nor below anywhere.
Of all forms yet formless,
self-luminous, it shines.
Whatever a being perceives
and thereby accumulates <s>karma</s> (action),
that becomes its destiny; therefore
one should contemplate the supportless.
There is no cause, there is no effect,
there is no <s>karma</s> by its own nature.
All this is unreal;
there is no world, no worldly being.
All this is supportless,
illuminated by the supportless.
Having made all this supportless,
one will become supportless.
One who does not meditate upon the great void,
sky-like and all-pervading,
remains a worldly being,
like a worm in a seed-pod.
For the arising of knowledge,
rituals and practices have been declared.
Abandoning <s>yoga</s> with supports,
one should contemplate the unmanifest.
From <s>Pātāla</s> (the netherworld) to <s>Śakti</s> (the highest power),
all that is desired —
those who have shattered it with the <s>mantra</s> of the void,
they are called knowers of the void.
The mind, greedy for sense objects,
is more restless even than a monkey.
Abiding in the state of total emptiness,
from there it will attain <s>nirvāṇa</s> (final liberation).
Undivided from all <s>tattvas</s> (principles), yet
distinct from the body as well,
undivided from the sense of 'I am', yet
consciousness facing in all directions.
Like space, all this,
both external and internal, O beloved —
seeing it as supreme bliss, formless,
one becomes a partaker of bliss.
Just as a fire without fuel
subsides of its own accord,
so the mind, in the absence of objects to grasp,
dissolves of its own accord.
Delusion, stupor, <s>māyā</s> (illusion),
and dream — these are fourfold.
Deep sleep and waking too —
all of these should be abandoned.
From the body, from the subtle <s>prāṇa</s> (breath),
from mind, from intellect, from <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego) —
'I am distinct from all of these' —
contemplating thus, one attains pure consciousness.
The mind is always overcome
by sleep, memory, and such.
Having awakened it with effort,
one should restore it to its natural state again and again.
When the mind becomes steady,
not wavering in any way,
one should not think of anything there;
one should simply keep it steady.
The mind seeks a support and a basis;
likewise, one should make it supportless.
The restless should be made motionless;
the motionless should not be disturbed.
When the dissolution of all elements occurs,
whatever pure space remains,
one should meditate on one's own form as that,
pervading and pure.
That alone is the fruit of birth,
that alone is true learning —
that the mind, restless like the moving wind,
is indeed held motionless.
One should not fix the mind above,
nor in the middle, nor below anywhere.
Free from all internal ideation,
one should always keep it supportless.
In sleep, one should awaken the mind;
when distracted, one should calm it again.
When both sides have been abandoned
and equilibrium is reached, one should not disturb it.
The mind, always supportless,
devoid of all bases,
freed from the states of mind —
that should be known as the mark of liberation.
Having held the mind in the heart,
empty of all supports,
whatever clear knowledge arises,
one should be devoted to its practice.
Those who meditate on the supreme void,
partless, without any fixed state,
they reach the supreme abode,
free from birth and death.
Gods and goddesses and others,
<s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) and their fruits,
the knowledge of support and the supported —
these are the bondage of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence).
Support is called duality;
from the abandonment of duality arises the Supreme.
The <s>yogī</s> is then liberated while living;
upon leaving the body, one is fully released.
The wise one should not abandon the body
through <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion) forcefully.
When actions cease from their very inception,
it will perish of its own accord.
In the lotus of the heart, the consciousness
that is of the nature of 'I', pure and immovable —
through the abandonment of <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego),
that consciousness becomes the bestower of liberation.
That which is free from all limiting adjuncts,
of the nature of pure consciousness, uninterrupted —
meditating 'That <s>Śiva</s> am I,'
one should relinquish all attachment.
The notions bound by region, caste, and such,
associated with <s>varṇa</s> (social class) and <s>āśrama</s> (life-stage) —
abandoning all these conceptions,
the wise one should contemplate one's own true nature.
I am one alone; no one belongs to me,
nor do I belong to anyone else.
I do not see anyone to whom I belong;
I do not see anyone who belongs to me.
I alone am the supreme <s>Brahman</s>,
lord of the universe, <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord).
Thus being certain, one is liberated;
thinking otherwise, a person remains bound.
When one sees the self as bodiless
through the eye of knowledge,
then one becomes peaceful in soul,
free from craving in every way.
He who is read about in all <s>śāstras</s> (scriptures)
as the unborn Lord,
bodiless, without qualities, the <s>Ātman</s> (Self) —
that am I, without a doubt.
Being pure consciousness alone, forever pure,
everywhere and always liberated,
neither to be accepted nor rejected, I am beyond reasoning;
therefore I am ever of the nature of <s>Brahman</s>, free from sorrow.
From the crown of the head to the soles of the feet,
within and without, wrapped in the sheath of skin —
all of that is of the nature of immortality; other than that
is the <s>Ātman</s> (Self), of the nature of consciousness, self-established.
I am the Lord of this moving and unmoving world,
the father and the mother and the grandfather.
Established in meditation, in the fourth state,
those who desire liberation meditate upon Me alone.
By <s>Brahmā</s> and other gods, by humans and <s>Nāgas</s>,
by hosts of <s>Gandharvas</s>, <s>Yakṣas</s>, and <s>Apsarases</s>,
through countless sacrifices, I alone am to be worshipped;
all of them worship Me alone.
Through fierce austerities and various forms of charity,
all of them worship Me alone.
I am all beings, both stationary and moving;
whatever others exist, I am all of them.
Neither gross nor subtle, nor of the form of void,
of the nature of knowledge alone, the sole kinsman of the world,
uninterrupted, pure, I am the Lord,
beyond the states of dream and others, unmanifest.
Beginningless awareness, unborn, ancient,
dwelling in the cave of the heart, partless, beyond manifestation,
unstained, incomparable, lordless,
invisible, ungraspable, of inconceivable form —
the eternal <s>Brahman</s>, uninterrupted —
at every step one should perceive 'That am I.'
One who abides thus in contemplation, unwavering,
becomes <s>Brahman</s> itself and attains immortality.
Thus, O beautiful one, <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge)
has been taught for the attainment of liberation.
Now hear from me
the <s>ācāra</s> (conduct) being spoken of.
No bathing, no <s>japa</s> (recitation), no worship,
<s>homa</s> (fire offering) is not a means either.
Fire rituals and other such rites —
none of these exist for such a one, O <s>Maheśvarī</s>.
Nor are there any observances for such a one,
nor service at sacred seats and <s>pīṭhas</s> (shrine seats).
No image-worship, no ancestral rites,
no pilgrimage, no <s>vratas</s> (vows).
There is no fruit of <s>dharma</s> (merit) or <s>adharma</s> (demerit);
no <s>tithis</s> (lunar days), no worldly rituals.
One should abandon all actions
and worldly conduct entirely.
All conventional observances without exception,
all prescribed duties are bondage.
Intention and conceptual thought,
and whoever else follows clan duties,
and <s>siddhis</s> (supernatural powers) of various kinds —
Elixirs of the netherworld and the like,
even if obtainable through direct perception,
the practitioner (<s>sādhaka</s>) should never grasp them.
All of them are bonds of the bound soul (<s>paśu</s>),
leading to the downward path.
Through these there is no supreme liberation,
without the all-pervading nature of consciousness (<s>cidrūpa</s>).
By whatever distinction,
the yogin maintaining yoga in all states,
should avoid, out of caution regarding the sacred sites (<s>kṣetrapīṭha</s>),
any curiosity.
Worms, insects, and moths,
and likewise, O <s>Devī</s>, trees —
the wise one should not destroy living beings,
since his mind is fixed on the supreme truth.
One should not uproot plants,
one should avoid cutting leaves,
one should not cause distress to beings,
nor the cutting of flowers.
With flowers that have fallen by themselves,
one should perform the worship of <s>Śiva</s>.
Killing, expulsion, and the like,
as well as enmity and immobilization,
fever, possession by spirits and ghosts,
subjugation, attraction, and bewilderment —
one should not perform such petty rites (<s>kṣudrakarma</s>),
nor the worship of wood and stone.
Equal toward enemy and friend,
equal toward a clod of earth and gold,
desire should never be entertained
toward the objects of the senses.
The yogin should delight in the self,
fearless and free from craving,
equal in blame and praise,
and equal toward all beings.
An equal vision should be maintained —
as toward oneself, so toward others.
Disputes, worldly assemblies,
and quarrels should be avoided.
One should not engage in debates on <s>śāstras</s>,
nor in ill-spoken or well-spoken words.
Jealousy, slander, and arrogance,
desire, envy,
lust, anger, fear, and grief —
one should renounce all these, gradually.
Free from all dualities,
always secluded from people,
in this very body,
being omniscient, one shines forth.
Just as liberation comes through knowledge alone,
so <s>siddhi</s> (supernatural power) is purposeless.
Nevertheless, those desiring enjoyment,
practitioners seek <s>siddhi</s>.
The attainment of qualities like <s>aṇimā</s> (becoming minute) and the rest —
whether it arises or does not arise,
even so, the embodied one is liberated,
having known the Lord (<s>Pati</s>) as pure.
The body is composed of the five elements;
<s>Śiva</s> abides within it.
From <s>Śiva</s> down to the earth,
this entire world is of the nature of <s>Śaṅkara</s>.
Those people who, seeing
such a knower, worship him
with incense, flowers, fruit, fragrant smoke,
bathing, garments, and food —
whoever offers these
through the actions of speech, mind, and body,
they too are liberated,
those who aspire to the path of liberation.
Those who praise or blame him
shall reap merit and sin respectively.
The conduct of knowledge that you asked about —
all of that has been told by me.
The knowledge of time, O Beautiful One —
what else do you wish to ask?
